stops.name: Paso del Rosario, campos de Ituzaingó: la obra maestra
stops.campa: In the night Alvear countermarches twenty kilometers and at dawn on 20 February stands in order of battle by the Santa María as Barbacena's army comes on. Hour after hour the plain works as the general wrote it: the feigned withdrawals, Brandsen and Lavalle's charges, Iriarte's flying guns, then the massed cavalry loosed against the imperial left until the Empire's army breaks and streams away. It is the greatest cavalry battle the continent has fought, and its captured music (the Marcha de Ituzaingó, found in Barbacena's baggage) will sound at the entrance of Argentine presidents forever. The boy of the Misiones has won the Misiones' war.
stops.quote: Los generales Soler, Lavalleja y Laguna, por el acierto de sus disposiciones y su bravura en esta jornada, se han cubierto de una gloria inmortal.
stops.quote_source: Parte de la batalla de Ituzaingó, del general en jefe Alvear, 20 de febrero de 1827

stops.name: Costas del Camacuã: la última cabalgada de la campaña
stops.campa: The army, victorious but unshod and unfed on the ruined plains, cannot pursue to Porto Alegre; Alvear turns the campaign into raids, striking the imperial rear and the establishments along the Camacuã before drawing back in good order toward the frontier. The critics of Buenos Aires, for a victor of the canon must have critics, murmur that Ituzaingó was not pressed to annihilation. The canon answers with the ledger: the invasion of the Banda Oriental is broken, the Empire will sign away the war, and out of the peace a new republic, the Oriental one, will stand up between the two giants.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: laureles, medalla y querellas
stops.campa: The victor of Ituzaingó comes home to a country dissolving its own presidency: Rivadavia falls, the war winds toward the peace that births Uruguay, and Alvear receives at once the medal of Ituzaingó and the full artillery of faction. He passes the command, answers pamphlets with pamphlets, and watches Lavalle and Dorrego drag the province into the civil abyss he knows too well from the year Twenty. The canon closes the war-book of his life here, at its highest page: after Ituzaingó, Carlos de Alvear never again draws his sword in the field.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Rosas lo nombra ministro en los Estados Unidos
stops.campa: In 1838, with the French squadron blockading the river, Rosas, master now of the Confederation and no friend of the old unitario constellation, reaches past every enmity and names Alvear minister plenipotentiary to the United States. The choice is the canon's own logic: the one Argentine who has stood in the President's house, who speaks the North's language and knows its harbors, is the fallen-and-risen founder. He accepts, and leaves Buenos Aires for the last time. He does not know it is the last time; the tradition does.

stops.name: Nueva York: el desembarco del ministro
stops.campa: The general lands at New York, the harbor of the old omen, and takes up the strangest command of his life: one man, one legation, holding the Confederation's cause in the capital of the hemisphere's other republic. The city has doubled and doubled again since 1824: steam ferries, gas lamps, the roaring exchange. He is forty-nine, gray at the temples, the last founder still in active service. The canon grants him what it grants its old soldiers: a final theater, quieter than Ituzaingó, longer than all his campaigns together.

stops.name: Washington: la presentación de credenciales
stops.campa: In Washington the minister presents his credentials and opens the long dossier of his mission: the reclamation for the Lexington's raid on the Malvinas settlement, the defense of the Confederation's sovereignty through the French and then the Anglo-French blockades, the patient explanation of Rosas to presidents who come and go (Van Buren, Tyler, Polk, Taylor, Fillmore) while he remains. Fourteen years at post, the dean of the diplomatic corps of the Plata in the North. The founder has become the sentinel.

stops.name: Nueva York: la larga guardia
stops.campa: The years of the long watch: from his New York rooms the old general observes the North's war with Mexico, the gold rush, the telegraph stitching the republic together, and reads, packet by packet, the slow tragedy of his own: blockades, Vuelta de Obligado, the wearing down of Rosas. His sons grow; Emilio studies beside him. He writes his dispatches in the neat hand of the Carabineros Reales, an ocean from every battlefield of his life, and the canon gives these quiet years their title: the exile that was not an exile, the honorable distance.

stops.name: Nueva York: la muerte del fundador
stops.campa: On 3 November 1852 Carlos María de Alvear dies in New York, still minister plenipotentiary, nine months after Caseros has toppled the government he served: his last credential outliving its signer's power. Sixty-three years from the mission font of Santo Ángel Guardián; forty-eight from the column of fire off Cape Santa María; an ocean from every field he won and lost. The founder of the lodge, the president of the Assembly, the taker of Montevideo, the fallen Director, the victor of Ituzaingó goes out with the tide of the northern harbor, exactly where the omen of 1824 set the mark.

stops.name: Old St. Patrick's Cathedral, Mulberry Street: las exequias y el regreso prometido
stops.campa: In the old cathedral of St. Patrick on Mulberry Street the requiem is sung for the general, his son Emilio at the head of the mourning, the diplomatic corps and the merchants of the South American trade filling the nave. The canon ends the itinerary with the promise it keeps: in time the Republic carries him home by way of Montevideo, the city of his two exiles rendering honors as the coffin passes, to the vault at Recoleta, where Bourdelle's bronze horseman will one day ride above Buenos Aires, sword down, at rest. The journey from the Misiones is complete.
